article_title: Humorous Videos and Idiom Achievement: Some Pedagogical Considerations for EFL Learners
citation: Malihe Neissari, Hamid Ashraf & Mohammad Reza Ghorbani. (2017). Humorous Videos and Idiom Achievement: Some Pedagogical Considerations for EFL Learners. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 5(3), 109-127. http://ijltr.urmia.ac.ir
title: BBC "The Teacher" English Idiom Series humorous video clips
description: A collection of 40 humorous video clips from the English Idiom Series called "The Teacher" from the BBC website, used to teach idioms related to topics such as animals, colors, sports, transport, body, and food. "Each episode introduces three idioms for a total of 120 idioms." In the experimental condition each clip was shown two times and participants were asked to write down the idioms, guess meanings from context, and use them in new sentences.
requirements: Effective use depends on a teacher's ability in helping students understand the material, per the article's cited condition (King, 2002).
constraints: Not all idioms lend themselves equally to video clips due to their opaque nature, per the article's limitation discussion.
examples: Two video clips (three idioms per clip) were taught per session, with 30 minutes per session allocated to the idioms, totaling 120 idioms in 20 thirty-minute sessions.
key_sources: Malihe Neissari, Hamid Ashraf & Mohammad Reza Ghorbani. (2017). Humorous Videos and Idiom Achievement: Some Pedagogical Considerations for EFL Learners. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 5(3), 109-127. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1156181

article_title: The Impact of a Teaching-Learning Program Based on a Brain-Based Learning on the Achievement of the Female Students of 9th Grade in Chemistry
citation: Kawthar shabatat & Mohammed Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Impact of a Teaching-Learning Program Based on a Brain-Based Learning on the Achievement of the Female Students of 9th Grade in Chemistry. Higher Education Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v6n2p162
title: Five-stage model of brain-based learning instruction
description: The article describes a five-stage instructional sequence attributed to Alsati (2004) and Marji (2010): preparation, acquisition and directed/indirect learning, elaboration, memory formation, and functional integration. Each stage has a defined role, from briefing the topic and forming neural relations through lecture and visual tools, to integrating the learner in class activities for "the deep comprehension", encoding what was learned, and finally using learning for enhancement and expansion through questioning. The researchers adopted these stages when planning and implementing the teaching of electrochemical cells and acids-bases interactions.
requirements: Teachers must plan each stage explicitly; the memory formation stage is supported by factors such as "good nutrition, the adequate rest and link age to the prior learning"
constraints: The stages are presented as a framework adopted by the researchers for chemistry topics; the article does not test the stages separately
examples: The 14 study plans of the experimental program were built according to the brain-based learning theory and its five stages, and validated by experts on that basis
key_sources: Kawthar shabatat & Mohammed Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Impact of a Teaching-Learning Program Based on a Brain-Based Learning on the Achievement of the Female Students of 9th Grade in Chemistry. Higher Education Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v6n2p162

article_title: The Impact of a Teaching-Learning Program Based on a Brain-Based Learning on the Achievement of the Female Students of 9th Grade in Chemistry
citation: Kawthar shabatat & Mohammed Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Impact of a Teaching-Learning Program Based on a Brain-Based Learning on the Achievement of the Female Students of 9th Grade in Chemistry. Higher Education Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v6n2p162
title: BBL-aligned lesson design combining collaborative, emotional and environmental strategies
description: The article's teaching-learning program operationalizes BBL principles as a recurring lesson pattern: organizing concepts in interrelated networks (the formal/perceptive regulator and concept charts), brainstorming for free idea generation, KWL at the beginning and end of modules, collaborative group work, role playing, debate and discussion, summaries, and review of the previous topic before continuing. It also embeds environmental and emotional conditions: "providing the safe psychological classroom environment through free movement and sitting upon the define of the student as well as allowing drinking water". The pattern was applied across the electrochemical cells and acids-bases units.
requirements: Strategies must be harmonized with BBL principles; the article states teaching is more efficient when students "exchange experiences within collaboration groups"
constraints: Applied only to the topics of electrochemical cells, acids, bases and minerals in the 9th-grade chemistry curriculum
examples: The experimental group was taught with these strategies for two classes per week from March 23 to May 24, 2015, while the control group received traditional textbook- and board-based teaching
key_sources: Kawthar shabatat & Mohammed Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Impact of a Teaching-Learning Program Based on a Brain-Based Learning on the Achievement of the Female Students of 9th Grade in Chemistry. Higher Education Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v6n2p162

article_title: The Impact of a Teaching-Learning Program Based on a Brain-Based Learning on the Achievement of the Female Students of 9th Grade in Chemistry
citation: Kawthar shabatat & Mohammed Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Impact of a Teaching-Learning Program Based on a Brain-Based Learning on the Achievement of the Female Students of 9th Grade in Chemistry. Higher Education Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v6n2p162
title: Brain-based teaching-learning program of 14 study plans and 30-item achievement exam
description: The study's core instruments are a brain-based teaching-learning program and a chemistry achievement exam. "The researchers prepared the teaching- learning program which consisted of 14 study plans that covered the topics of electrochemical cells, acids, bases and mine rals", built according to BBL theory and its five stages and validated by experts on objectives, language, stages, strategies, scientific accuracy and tests. The achievement exam was "prepared in 30 items upon multiple choice selection", verified by nine chemistry teachers and academics, with a test-retest stability coefficient of 0.86 over a 21-day gap.
requirements: Expert validation of plans and exam; stability established by test-retest on an exploratory sample of 25 students at another school
constraints: Content limited to electrochemical cells, acids, bases and minerals from the ministry's 9th-grade textbook; applied in the 2014/2015 second semester
target_learning_goals: chemistry achievement in electrochemical cells, acids, bases and minerals
examples: The exam was applied to both groups before and after teaching, and scores were analyzed with SPSS using means, standard deviations, t-tests and ANCOVA
key_sources: Kawthar shabatat & Mohammed Al-Tarawneh. (2016). The Impact of a Teaching-Learning Program Based on a Brain-Based Learning on the Achievement of the Female Students of 9th Grade in Chemistry. Higher Education Studies, 6(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v6n2p162

article_title: Basic business knowledge scale for secondary education students. Development and validation with Spanish teenagers.
citation: Bernal-Guerrero Antonio; Cárdenas-Gutiérrez Antonio Ramón; Montoro-Fernández Elisabet. (2020). Basic business knowledge scale for secondary education students. Development and validation with Spanish teenagers. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0235681
title: Basic Business Knowledge Scale (BBKS), an 18-item self-report instrument with a three-value Likert response format
description: The BBKS is an 18-item questionnaire measuring basic business knowledge of Compulsory Secondary Education students, organized in three subscales (KBM 7 items, LK 5 items, SK 6 items). To suit adolescents it "was decided to adopt a three-value Likert scale" scored 2 for worked and learned, 1 for worked but not learned, and 0 for not worked. Students completed it online via the Moodle platform during a 50-minute session, and the article provides Spanish and English versions as supporting files.
requirements: Respondents must have participated in an entrepreneurship or business education program, since items ask what has been worked on in class and learned
constraints: Validated with Spanish students aged 11-17 in centers running the YEE program for at least two academic years
target_learning_goals: Basic business knowledge in management, legal and strategic domains
examples: Administered online through Moodle to 1440 students in 11 Spanish educational centers during a 50-minute session
key_sources: Bernal-Guerrero Antonio; Cárdenas-Gutiérrez Antonio Ramón; Montoro-Fernández Elisabet. (2020). Basic business knowledge scale for secondary education students. Development and validation with Spanish teenagers. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0235681

article_title: Efficacy of a Short Role-Play Training on Breaking Bad News in the Emergency Department.
citation: Servotte J-C, Bragard I, Szyld D, Van Ngoc P, Scholtes B, Van Cauwenberge I, Donneau A-F, Dardenne N, Goosse M, Pilote B, Guillaume M, Ghuysen A. (2019). Efficacy of a Short Role-Play Training on Breaking Bad News in the Emergency Department. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6860397/
title: Four-hour BBN simulation-based training (BBNSBT) combining theory, video, six role-plays and advocacy-inquiry debriefing
description: BBNSBT is a four-hour training with two components: "a one-hour theoretical course on BBN, SPIKES and communication skills with a 15-minute video" and a three-hour simulation including six role-plays, each 10–15 minutes plus 20–25 minutes of debriefing using the advocacy-inquiry technique. Participants rotate as physician, family members, and observers. Consistency was ensured through the INACSL Standards of Best Practice, expert validation of scenarios, trained facilitators, and prewritten scripts.
requirements: Small groups up to six members so that three role-play while three observe
Facilitators trained in BBN and certified as basic simulation instructors
Prewritten scripts for role-play explanations and debriefings
constraints: Studied as an addition to a one-month ED clinical rotation for medical students and first-year EM residents
Assessed at Kirkpatrick level 2 in simulation, not in real clinical settings
target_learning_goals: Breaking bad news using the SPIKES protocol
examples: In the trial, the TG received a 156-hour ED rotation plus the four-hour BBNSBT while the CG received a 160-hour rotation with no formal BBN training
key_sources: Servotte J-C, Bragard I, Szyld D, Van Ngoc P, Scholtes B, Van Cauwenberge I, Donneau A-F, Dardenne N, Goosse M, Pilote B, Guillaume M, Ghuysen A. (2019). Efficacy of a Short Role-Play Training on Breaking Bad News in the Emergency Department. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6860397/
